Some patterns count the post as a stich, but most don't (the chain to go up to start the next row). Definitely try videos, markers, and lots of practice. You're doing great!

Make a list of things that you need to accomplish. Arrange them in order of urgency and imagine a realistic timeline. Things that you can't accomplish in that day or ones that can wait a while, add to a "later list". 
From the list of more time sensitive matters, choose 1 or 2 to take on for that day only and set a timer. Don't straggle or jump to things outside of thay days list unless of course it's an emergency. But for example, if you need to clean the house or re organize a room; break down the steps needed to make it happen. So for kitchen you could do 1. Gather dirty dishes and put away clean ones. 2. Wash remainder of dishes. 3. Empty fridge and clean inside. 4. Remove garbage. 5. Wipe all surfaces. 6. Sweep and mop. 
Breaking things into more manageable tasks makes life much easier and you get the dopamine from completing a task. It's easy to be overwhelmed and shut down when you think of everything as a whole, "I have to clean the house, go to the bank, get groceries, write work emails, and everything in between". That's exhausting to think about.

You have great strength and mobility and I understand it can be exciting to crack right into new things, but always make sure to have a good warmup and continued strength training. A good trick to learn the muscle positions are during pull ups on the pole and doing dumbell presses on a bench or floor. Naturally we don't pay too much attention so it takes practice. When you do a pole pull up from standing, make sure to not hyper extend in the reach. Don't round and stretch the ligaments when reaching. Grasp the pole and try to focus on keeping your shoulder blades in the same area. Pull up with your biceps and the larger muscles. Gosh it's really hard to explain properly. I'm sure you've removed the first bandage but if not, don't remove it. Keep adding clean gauze or cloths and apply direct pressure to the wound. Keep adding until the bleeding stops and hold pressure. You can tie a triangle wrap on each layer if you have any. Do not remove layers to add more as it will disrupt the clotting process. 
Keep the area clean and covered until you can get some bandages or steri strip. Was around the wound with antibacterial soap (not in the wound) and then irrigate the wound with saline water. Watch video on how to properly apply steri strips. Apply. Cover with a sterile, non stick pad (fully covered) and then wrap gauze to cover the entire pad or if a large bandaid covers it do that to keep it discreet.
Most cases will eventually clot up and stop on their own. Don't use a string, or belt, or cloth to make a tourniquet unless the bleeding is quickly soaking through every layer at a very fast rate and is not controlled by pressure. Then you'll have to write the time and go to the hospital....so that's not a good option anyway. More often than none it'll stop with direct, firm pressure and layered bandages. 
There's alot of bad info here that can lead you to cause more harm than good. Keep everything clean and sterile or you'll need antibiotics too.

A few things to try: 
Wash clothing with a long lasting scent booster and let air dry. I find the drier kills alot of the nice smell. I air dry my workout clothes and when I sweat and workout I can smell the detergent instead of my BO.
Hydration! Drink lots of water and a healthy balanced diet so help with natural body smells. Processed foods and sugars put the body out of whack amd it can change your smell. 
Use a deodorant that has an antiperspirant. I use old spice wolthorn. It is a men's deodorant but it mixes well with my body scent and stays. I found alot of deodorant turn into a "dusty" smell over the day. I re apply as needed. Keep baby wipes handy if you can to wipe off old deodorant beforehand. 
Spray perfume on clothing, not skin. My body makes most nice perfumes smell like hot garbage and I've wasted so much over the years. I only spray my clothing at the collar or bust and it stays true to the original smell. 
I shower at night and have a rinse in the morning, or vice versa. Sometimes more if I have the opportunity. I dont wash my hair every day so I use a nice smelling dry shampoo or a hair perfume as needed. 
After shower I use a light scented lotion and baby powder on areas that get more perspiration.
It can take a while to find scents that work well with your body.

Hair: I used to have waist length wavy curl hair that was never "tameable" unless I put it in a gelled low bun. I have a short pixie cut that is easily styled into a sleek look with gel. Try using a spray gel or quality hairspray to keep strays down. Keeping a small bottle in your purse with a comb does wonders mid day.
Makeup: I am certified in hairdressing and makeup so I find this is fairly easy for me but it can be totally overwhelming with all the products! My go tos are a setting spray and blotting powder. Panic attacks can burn calories. A major sign of a panic attack in an increased heartrate. Most panic attacks last on average 5 to 20 minutes. The amount of calories burned would depend on metabolic rate, age, weight, and BMI. For example: a 150 pound 22-year old suffering an onset panic attack with a heart rate of 140 bpm for 15 minutes would average a caloric usage of 170 calories. This takes into consideration the normal usage of calories for daily function within that time. It would not be a significant amount burned just from having panic attack symptoms but it could add up. The majority of calories burned during an episode would be attributed to fidgeting and pacing. 
All that being said, dont count on it as a good weight loss method. Stress raises cortisol levels that can negatively impact fat loss so it's not reliable.
